source: Kaiser et al. (2025) CogniLoad benchmark
finding: Synthetic logic puzzles map CLT onto three knobs: intrinsic difficulty d (number of interacting people, attributes, values and rule complexity), distractor ratio, and task length N. 22 reasoning LLMs tested. Task length N was the dominant stressor, more than d.
numbers: 1,400 puzzles per configuration. Accuracy fell with d for most models; by d=5, 12 of 22 models were under 50%. Beyond d about 7 the decline flattened. gpt-5 0.96 to 0.93 from d=1 to d=3 and 0.82 at d=10; o3 0.80 at d=10. Distilled models lost 0.10-0.25 from d=1 to d=3.
limits: Closest direct test of element interactivity in LLMs. d bundles several facets (state space, rule complexity), so it is not a pure interacting-element count. Length N is confounded with sequential updating. No human group.
agent_relevance: Strong models tolerate d up to about 7-10 but weaker ones fail at d=3-5. Expect a model-specific interactivity ceiling and measure it, not assume it.

source: Kaiser et al. (2025) CogniLoad: capacity points
finding: The paper defines ID50, the maximum intrinsic complexity (interacting entities and attributes) a model handles at 50% accuracy, plus ECL50 for context length. Small models never reach 50%.
numbers: gpt-5 and o3 lead with ECL50 above 300 statements. Phi-4-mini-reasoning, DS-Qwen-1.5B and Qwen3-1.7B do not reach 50% under mean conditions. Steepest drop for most models is N=20 to N=50 (DS-Llama-70B 0.89 to 0.66; Qwen3-8B 0.71 to 0.40); gpt-5 1.00 to 0.98.
limits: Values come from a GLM fit, so for models far from the threshold they are extrapolated.
agent_relevance: A per-model capacity number is usable as the S0 gate: split when estimated interacting elements exceed the model's own capacity.

source: Kaiser et al. (2025) CogniLoad: failure modes
finding: Under load, errors shift to tracking sequential state updates, and 'other' failures rise with length in small and mid-tier models. Distractor ratio gives a U-shaped accuracy curve (dip at 10-25% needle share for many models).
numbers: At N=100 the strongest models are nearly flat across distractor ratio (about 0.93-0.97). At N=250 most curves are flat.
limits: The U-shape explanation is the authors' own. No human control.
agent_relevance: Long chains of state updates fail before single hard steps do. Break long chains with checkpointed state summaries.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Beyond Accuracy: cognitive load framework for tool-use agents (ToolLoad-Bench)
finding: Intrinsic load of an agent task is the structure of its Tool Interaction Graph (a DAG of tool calls with dependency edges), summed over edge loads. 500 task instances with tunable load. Accuracy drops steadily as intrinsic load rises; general models collapse at high load.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o (68.0% overall), GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Qwen3-8B/32B/235B, Llama3.3-70B, xLAM2-32B (78.8%, best). At high intrinsic load only xLAM2-32B stays above 60%. Llama3.3-70B is at 23% even at low load.
limits: Edge weights chosen and fitted by the authors; 500 synthetic instances. The best model was fine-tuned for tool use, so load tolerance can be trained.
agent_relevance: An agent can score its own plan by the number of dependent calls and joins before running it, then decompose if the score is high.

source: Wang et al. (2026) ToolLoad-Bench: load-success model
finding: Fits a logistic model: success probability depends on total load (intrinsic plus weighted extraneous). Each model gets a slope k (sensitivity to load) and baseline b. Calibration checked with Hosmer-Lemeshow and plots.
numbers: xLAM2-32B has the lowest k and a very low b. GPT-4o has low sensitivity but a higher baseline. Qwen3-8B has a weaker baseline and higher sensitivity than Qwen3-235B. Ambiguous queries and distractor tools cut accuracy for all models.
limits: Weight of extraneous versus intrinsic is set to match accuracy drops, so the two scales are not independent.
agent_relevance: Supports a per-model load budget with a measured slope. Ambiguity and structure both cost accuracy: clean the prompt and split the structure.

source: Fesser, Ektefaie, Fang, Kakade, Zitnik (2026, ICML) Evaluating Relational Reasoning in LLMs with REL
finding: Relational complexity (RC) is the minimum number of independent entities that must be bound at once to apply a relation (Halford et al. 1998). Performance falls monotonically with RC even when entity count is fixed, so entity count is a noisy proxy.
numbers: Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro Preview, GPT 5.2. Raven matrices and tensors: 45% drop when RC goes 3 to 9. Biology REL-B1: RC 5 to 20 cuts accuracy by 93%. Chemistry: task completion falls 39.7% from C1 to C3. RC explains the largest share of explainable variance: 24% Claude, 32% Gemini, 44% GPT.
limits: Three models. RC is the Halford arity measure, related to but not the same as Sweller's element interactivity.
agent_relevance: Best match for our gate: count how many items must be held jointly in one step (arity), not how many items are in the input.

source: Fesser et al. (2026) REL: inference-time interventions
finding: More thinking tokens, one-shot examples, best-of-N and majority vote did not fix high-RC failure. This points to a binding limit, not a shortage of steps.
numbers: Token cap 4,096 to 16,384 gave about 2-3% on REL-A and about 0.4% on REL-C. One-shot ICL on REL-C: C1 77.0% (+6.6), C2 43.3% (+3.4), C3 32.7% (+6.0), ordering unchanged. REL-B1, GPT-5.2, 5 runs, 15 questions per level: best-of-5 46.7 to 60.0% at 4 hosts but 0 to 6.7% at 25; majority vote 46.7 to 40.0% at 4 and 20.0 to 6.7% at 10.
limits: The best-of-N and vote test is a small exploratory sample (15 questions per level).
agent_relevance: Sampling and voting will not rescue a step with too many jointly bound items. Only changing the structure (decompose) can. Favors O3 over more samples.

source: Fesser et al. (2026) REL: low versus high RC on matrices
finding: With RC of 1 or 2 all three models are near perfect even on 30x30 matrices. When RC grows with input size (REL-A3, A4) they collapse.
numbers: About 91% at RC 1-2 on 30x30. Claude and Gemini fall to about 12% on REL-A3 30x30; GPT-5.2 drops nearly 40%. On REL-A4 only GPT-5.2 is non-trivial (21% on 9x9). Adding digits per entry (5 to 10) cost only 1-6%.
limits: Operand size effects are small here but the paper does not test every size factor.
agent_relevance: Large but low-interactivity inputs are fine. Small high-arity steps are not. Gate on arity, not length.

source: Adapala (2025) Cognitive Load Limits in LLMs: Benchmarking Multi-Hop Reasoning (ICE)
finding: Interleaved Cognitive Evaluation varies extraneous load (20/50/80% irrelevant tokens) and task switching on 2- and 3-hop questions. Small models fail completely on the high-intrinsic-load task.
numbers: 200 questions x 10 replications. Llama-3-8B, Llama-3-70B, Mistral-7B all 0% in every condition, even clean control. Gemini-2.0-Flash 0.85 control, 0.82 at 20%, 0.78 at 50%, 0.72 at 80% (beta -0.003 per % load, p<0.001). Long control 0.82 equals control (p=0.45), so length alone is not the cause. GPT-4o 0.65 to 0.55, not significant (p=0.07), confounded by truncation. Residue effect not significant (p=0.12).
limits: Independent author, preprint, 2024-era models. Measures extraneous load more than intrinsic load.
agent_relevance: A hard multi-hop item can be a floor effect for weak models, so decomposition or a stronger model is needed. Pruning irrelevant text helps capable models.

source: Zhang (2025) Cognitive Load-Aware Inference: Token Economy of LLMs (CLAI)
finding: Defines intrinsic load for LLMs through element interactivity and uses a meta-prompt (CLAI-Prompt): assess intrinsic load, decompose, drop irrelevant context, then allocate token budget. CLAI-Tune is a fine-tuned version. An LLM scaffold built directly on intrinsic load.
numbers: Llama-3-70B GSM8K: CoT 92.5% at 485 tokens vs CLAI-Prompt 92.3% at 310 tokens (-36.1%). MATH: 53.9% at 812 tokens vs 53.5% at 525 (-35.3%). Authors claim CLAI-Tune cuts tokens over 40% and beats CoT accuracy.
limits: Single author, no ablation separating the load-assessment step from generic decomposition, tuning data is synthetic, no independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Nearest existing version of the S0 gate plus O3 decompose idea. Gain is token savings with flat accuracy, so do not expect accuracy gains from the gate alone.

source: Upadhayay, Behzadan, Karbasi (2024) Cognitive Overload Attack: Prompt Injection for Long Context
finding: Applies CLT to in-context learning. Adding intrinsic and extraneous load (hidden tasks, task switching, obfuscation, graded CL0 to CL5) raises jailbreak success. Load is measured by judge LLMs, irrelevant-token output and benchmark scores.
numbers: Attack success up to 99.99% on the Forbidden Question set and 97% on JailbreakBench. Models: GPT-4, Claude-3.5 Sonnet, Claude-3 Opus, Llama-3-70B-Instruct, Gemini-1.0-Pro, Gemini-1.5-Pro.
limits: Load levels are designed by the authors and mix several manipulations. The link between load and safety failure is correlational. Not a measure of element interactivity.
agent_relevance: High-load prompts weaken guardrail adherence. Check guardrails after each decomposed step, not once on a loaded prompt.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025, ICLR) GSM-Symbolic
finding: Adding clauses (more interacting quantities) to grade-school problems lowers accuracy and raises variance in all tested models. The rate of drop also grows with each added clause.
numbers: Gemma2-9b-it: GSM-M1 84.4, GSM-Symbolic 79.1, P1 68.1, P2 41.8 (std 6.0). Other models show the same ordering.
limits: The authors note a clause is not exactly one reasoning step. Stronger models (o1-class) lose less. Contamination is another proposed cause.
agent_relevance: Each added interacting clause costs more than the last. Keep each step to few clauses.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025, ICLR) GSM-Symbolic: GSM-NoOp
finding: Adding one plausible but irrelevant statement (NoOp) makes models turn it into an operation. Few-shot examples of the same variants do not repair it.
numbers: Drops up to 65% across state-of-the-art models; more recent models fell more than older ones. Changing names matters little; changing numbers hurts more.
limits: No human baseline given. Some NoOp items are pragmatic traps.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant elements can become interacting elements. Strip them before reasoning.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Controlled puzzles (Tower of Hanoi, River Crossing, Checkers, Blocks World) scale complexity by number of elements. Three regimes: non-thinking models match or beat thinking models at low complexity, thinking wins at medium, both collapse at high.
numbers: Accuracy goes to near zero past a model-specific threshold (reasoning models begin to collapse at Hanoi N=7-8). Thinking tokens rise with complexity then fall near the collapse point despite unused budget. In one case failure comes before move 50 at N=12 while the same model passes 100+ moves at N=10.
limits: Disputed by Lawsen (2025). Solution length and compositional depth are confounded with number of interacting elements.
agent_relevance: More thinking budget may not rescue high-complexity steps. Decompose before the cliff.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking
finding: A comment arguing the collapse is mostly an artefact: Hanoi outputs hit token limits, River Crossing included impossible instances (N>5 with boat capacity 3), and scoring cannot tell inability from refusing to list long outputs.
numbers: Asked for a Lua function for 15-disk Hanoi, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4, o3 and Gemini 2.5 had very high accuracy in under 5,000 tokens. Plain move listing caps at about N=12-13 for 64,000 tokens.
limits: Short comment, not peer reviewed, no full table. Shojaee et al. reply that collapse starts at N=7-8, within limits.
agent_relevance: Separate complexity effects from output-length artefacts. Choose tasks where complexity is jointly bound items, not count of output steps.

source: Dziri et al. (2023, NeurIPS) Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality
finding: Models multiplication, logic grid puzzles and dynamic programming as computation graphs and measures complexity by graph depth and width. Accuracy falls toward zero as complexity rises, even after fine-tuning. Models seem to match subgraphs seen in training.
numbers: Off-the-shelf ChatGPT 55% and GPT-4 59% on 3-digit by 3-digit multiplication. Zero-shot accuracy falls to near zero at larger sizes for GPT-4, ChatGPT, LLaMA and FlanT5. Fine-tuned GPT-3 is near perfect in-domain and fails out of domain.
limits: 2023 models; newer reasoning models do much better on multiplication. The pattern-matching explanation is contested.
agent_relevance: Compositional depth and width predict failure. Supports decomposing into few-element subgraphs.

source: Zhou et al. (2023, ICLR) Least-to-Most Prompting
finding: Decompose a problem into sub-problems solved in order, each seeing earlier answers. Generalizes to problems harder than the demos.
numbers: Last-letter concatenation: list length 12 CoT 31.8% vs least-to-most 74.0%; length 4 84.2% vs 94.0%. SCAN length split: least-to-most 99.7% vs CoT 16.2% (first model column), with 76.0% and 60.7% in the other two columns where CoT scored 0.0.
limits: GPT-3-class models. Exemplars are hand written per task. Remaining errors are mostly concatenation errors, not the decomposed steps.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for O3: splitting into low-interactivity subproblems gives large gains on long compositional inputs.

source: Khot et al. (2023, ICLR) Decomposed Prompting
finding: A decomposer prompt writes a program of sub-tasks. Each goes to its own prompted handler, which can be decomposed further or replaced by a symbolic function. Tested on eight datasets with GPT-3.
numbers: Hard sub-tasks such as the kth letter of a string and list reversal are solved by recursive decomposition (reverse lists by halves down to length 3). I did not record the per-dataset gain over CoT from the tables.
limits: Needs hand-written prompts per task. The decomposition is fixed by the author, not found by the model.
agent_relevance: Pattern for O3: decompose until a sub-step has few elements, then call a tool or a fresh context for it.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) How Well Do LLMs Perform on the Simplest Long-Chain Reasoning Tasks: Equivalence Class Problem
finding: Task: say whether two variables are equal given random equivalence relations. Varies number of variables, connectivity and prompts. Non-reasoning models fail; reasoning models are much better but not perfect. Hardest cases sit near the connectivity phase transition.
numbers: DeepSeek-V3 and V3.2 error above 90% at n=144; Gemini-3-Flash about 22% at n=144. Non-reasoning error: depth 1 4.4%, depth 2 58%, depth 3 85%. DeepSeek-R1 error about 0.01% at shallow depth but still has spikes near the critical point, and putting 10 queries on one graph raised errors versus 1 query.
limits: Synthetic logic; no human baseline; few-shot examples helped little.
agent_relevance: Error rises sharply with chain depth and number of interacting variables. One question per context and reasoning mode help.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2024, AAAI) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study
finding: Verbal and spatial n-back on gpt-3.5-turbo (50 blocks each, n=1,2,3). Performance declines as n rises, like humans, and noise reduces it. The authors call this a working-memory capacity limit.
numbers: Capacity about 3 in verbal variants: sensitivity d' drops to about 1 at n=3. Noise lowers capacity.
limits: Contested by Hu and Lewis (2025). One main model. n-back also taxes task-set maintenance.
agent_relevance: If LLMs had a human-like capacity near 3 items, 'few elements per step' would be literal. The evidence is weak (next line).

source: Hu and Lewis (2025) Do Language Models Understand the Cognitive Tasks Given to Them? Investigations with the N-Back Paradigm
finding: Re-runs n-back on open-source models of varied strength. Poor 2-back and 3-back scores are at least partly a failure to understand the task and keep the task set, not a pure memory limit. The best model was pushed to 10-back with alternative prompts, followed by attention analysis.
numbers: I read the abstract and introduction only; no table numbers recorded.
limits: Open models only. Full result tables not read.
agent_relevance: Capacity claims from human paradigms must control task comprehension. Test our own element limit with clear instructions and examples first.

source: CausalBN-Bench (secondhand via search summary)
finding: A search summary says LLM performance on causal structure learning degrades once variables exceed about 50.
numbers: Threshold about 50 variables per the summary; not verified in the paper.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite the number without checking.
agent_relevance: Weak lead only.

source: CoThinker (2025) United Minds or Isolated Agents? Coordination of LLMs under Cognitive Load Theory
finding: Treats multi-constraint failure as intrinsic overload (task complexity plus element interactivity). Splits the work across agents with different thinking styles, a shared transactive memory and a communication moderator. Beat single-agent and debate baselines on LiveBench.
numbers: LiveBench average, normalized to Flash-8B IO=1.00. Flash-8B: IO 1.00, CoT 1.03, Self-Refine 0.75, MAD 0.97, DMAD 0.91, CoThinker 1.07. Flash: IO 1.53, CoThinker 1.70. Pro: IO 1.85, DMAD 2.05, CoThinker 2.09. Pro math 2.40 vs 2.00; data analysis 3.39 vs 2.92.
quote: intrinsic load (determined by task complexity and element interactivity)
limits: Gains are small on average (+0.04 to +0.24 normalized). Instruction following got worse (Pro 0.95 vs 1.03 IO). Intrinsic load is never measured, only argued. Main agent count not stated.
agent_relevance: Supports O3 decompose across differently-framed workers, but warns that coordination cost can hurt simple or format-bound tasks. Gate it on S0 load estimate.

source: CoThinker (2025) cross-model and ablation results
finding: On newer models, the multi-agent split helped most in a constrained setting. Removing thinking styles or the transactive memory cut math scores for some models; for GPT5-Nano, removing memory raised the score.
numbers: Constrained, Gemini-2.5 math/reasoning: CoThinker 76.3/69.2 vs IO 59.3/31.0. GPT-4.1: 40.0/70.8 vs 34.0/40.8. Standard: GPT-5 88.57/81.88 vs IO 82.63/68.38. Ablation full/no-styles/no-memory on math: Qwen3-30B 81.87/69.79/76.41; GPT5-Nano 55.97/49.02/62.36; GPT-OSS-20B 57.15/48.21/58.37. Best moderator N=2-3; agents M=6, rounds T=3 by default.
limits: Cross-model table partial. Agent count is non-monotonic. Newer GPT models sometimes refuse to show intermediate reasoning, weakening the memory.
agent_relevance: The decomposition benefit is largest when the task is hard for the model (reasoning 31.0 to 69.2). Small, easy tasks gain little. Supports a hardness-triggered split.

source: CoThinker (2025) load proxies
finding: Uses attention entropy and perplexity as diagnostic proxies of overload. Perplexity of the answer fell when the team structure was added.
numbers: Perplexity (baseline / styles / memory / references N=3): Qwen3-8B 6.56 / 3.58 / 1.69 / 3.10. Mistral-7B 6.63 / 5.04 / 1.58 / 2.86.
limits: Perplexity needs ground-truth answers, so it is unusable at inference. Overloaded models can be confidently wrong. Diagnostic only.
agent_relevance: No cheap inference-time load gauge exists here. S0 must estimate interactivity from the task text (count of interacting elements), not from model internals.
